prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: US International Trade in Goods and Services
Description: The U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services program is a monthly release providing comprehensive data on U.S. trade balance, exports, and imports. It covers physical goods and services, measuring international transactions.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

International Trade in Goods and Services

U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, August 2026

August 2026
-$105.6 B
July 2026
-$92.8 B

The U.S. goods and services trade deficit increased in August 2026 according to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis and the U.S. Census Bureau. The deficit increased from $92.8 billion in July (revised) to $105.6 billion in August, as imports increased more than exports. The goods deficit increased $12.8 billion in August to $136.6 billion. The services surplus increased less than $0.1 billion in August to $31.0 billion.

EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 8:30 a.m. EDT, Tuesday, October 6, 2026
BEA 26—44
CB 26—160

U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, August 2026

The U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis announced today that the goods and services deficit was $105.6 billion in August, up $12.7 billion from $92.8 billion in July, revised.

U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services Deficit
Deficit: $105.6 Billion +13.7%°
Exports: $315.2 Billion +1.4%°
Imports: $420.8 Billion +4.3%°

Next release: Wednesday, November 4, 2026

(°) Statistical significance is not applicable or not measurable. Data adjusted for seasonality but not price changes

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, October 6, 2026

Exports, Imports, and Balance (exhibit 1)

August exports were $315.2 billion, $4.5 billion more than July exports. August imports were $420.8 billion, $17.2 billion more than July imports.

The August increase in the goods and services deficit reflected an increase in the goods deficit of $12.8 billion to $136.6 billion and an increase in the services surplus of less than $0.1 billion to $31.0 billion.

Year-to-date, the goods and services deficit decreased $138.2 billion, or 19.9 percent, from the same period in 2025. Exports increased $267.7 billion or 11.8 percent. Imports increased $129.5 billion or 4.4 percent.

Three-Month Moving Averages (exhibit 2)

The average goods and services deficit increased $9.9 billion to $89.9 billion for the three months ending in August.

  • Average exports decreased $1.6 billion to $314.4 billion in August.
  • Average imports increased $8.3 billion to $404.3 billion in August.

Year-over-year, the average goods and services deficit increased $25.4 billion from the three months ending in August 2025.

  • Average exports increased $31.1 billion from August 2025.
  • Average imports increased $56.5 billion from August 2025.

Exports (exhibits 3, 6, and 7)

Exports of goods increased $4.4 billion to $205.7 billion in August.

  Exports of goods on a Census basis increased $4.2 billion.

  • Industrial supplies and materials increased $6.3 billion.
    • Nonmonetary gold increased $2.3 billion.
    • Crude oil increased $2.0 billion.
    • Fuel oil increased $1.2 billion.
  • Capital goods increased $1.3 billion.
    • Semiconductors increased $1.0 billion.
    • Computers increased $0.9 billion.
    • Computer accessories increased $0.9 billion.
    • Civilian aircraft decreased $1.0 billion.
  • Consumer goods decreased $2.2 billion.
    • Pharmaceutical preparations decreased $2.4 billion.

  Net balance of payments adjustments increased $0.3 billion.

Treatment of Gold in BEA’s International and National Economic Accounts

When incorporating the statistics in this release into BEA’s National Economic Accounts, including Gross Domestic Product, or GDP, BEA replaces exports and imports of nonmonetary gold with an adjustment calculated as the difference between domestic production and industrial use of gold. For additional information, see “How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts?” and “How are exports and imports of nonmonetary gold treated in BEA’s National Economic Accounts?”.

Exports of services increased less than $0.1 billion to $109.5 billion in August.

  • Charges for the use of intellectual property increased $0.2 billion.
  • Other business services increased $0.1 billion.
  • Travel decreased $0.2 billion.
  • Financial services decreased $0.1 billion.

Imports (exhibits 4, 6, and 8)

Imports of goods increased $17.2 billion to $342.2 billion in August.

  Imports of goods on a Census basis increased $17.4 billion.

  • Industrial supplies and materials increased $9.1 billion.
    • Crude oil increased $3.3 billion.
    • Nonmonetary gold increased $3.1 billion.
  • Capital goods increased $6.2 billion.
    • Semiconductors increased $2.4 billion.
    • Other industrial machinery increased $1.3 billion.
    • Computer accessories decreased $1.6 billion.

  Net balance of payments adjustments decreased $0.2 billion.

Imports of services increased less than $0.1 billion to $78.5 billion in August.

  • Transport increased $0.4 billion.
  • Charges for the use of intellectual property decreased $0.2 billion.
  • Travel decreased $0.1 billion.

Real Goods in 2017 Dollars – Census Basis (exhibit 11)

The real goods deficit increased $8.7 billion, or 8.2 percent, to $114.7 billion in August, compared to an 11.1 percent increase in the nominal deficit.

  • Real exports of goods increased $1.9 billion, or 1.3 percent, to $153.0 billion, compared to a 2.1 percent increase in nominal exports.
  • Real imports of goods increased $10.7 billion, or 4.1 percent, to $267.7 billion, compared to a 5.4 percent increase in nominal imports.

Revisions

Revisions to July exports

  • Exports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion.
  • Exports of services were revised down $0.2 billion.

Revisions to July imports

  • Imports of goods were revised up $4.4 billion.
  • Imports of services were revised down $0.2 billion.

Goods by Selected Countries and Areas: Monthly – Census Basis (exhibit 19)

The August figures show surpluses, in billions of dollars, with Netherlands ($7.7), South and Central America ($5.6), United Kingdom ($3.6), Hong Kong ($2.3), Brazil ($1.3), Belgium ($1.2), Australia ($0.6), and Saudi Arabia ($0.4). Deficits were recorded, in billions of dollars, with Mexico ($27.7), Vietnam ($24.0), Taiwan ($18.3), China ($16.4), European Union ($11.0), South Korea ($9.4), Canada ($7.1), India ($6.2), Germany ($6.2), Malaysia ($6.0), Italy ($4.3), Japan ($3.7), Ireland ($2.5), France ($1.4), Israel ($0.8), Switzerland ($0.4), and Singapore ($0.3).

  • The deficit with Canada increased $4.1 billion to $7.1 billion in August. Exports increased $0.5 billion to $29.9 billion and imports increased $4.6 billion to $37.1 billion.
  • The balance with Singapore shifted from a surplus of $1.9 billion in July to a deficit of $0.3 billion in August. Exports decreased $1.1 billion to $3.7 billion and imports increased $1.2 billion to $4.0 billion.
  • The deficit with Ireland decreased $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion in August. Exports increased $0.1 billion to $1.7 billion and imports decreased $1.4 billion to $4.2 billion.

All statistics referenced are seasonally adjusted; statistics are on a balance of payments basis unless otherwise specified. Additional statistics, including not seasonally adjusted statistics and details for goods on a Census basis, are available in exhibits 1-20b of this release. For information on data sources, definitions, and revision procedures, see the explanatory notes in this release. The full release can be found at www.census.gov/foreign-trade/Press-Release/current_press_release/index.html or www.bea.gov/data/intl-trade-investment/international-trade-goods-and-services. The full schedule is available in the Census Bureau’s Economic Briefing Room at www.census.gov/economic-indicators/ or on BEA’s website at www.bea.gov/news/schedule.

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: US International Trade in Goods and Services
Description: The U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services program is a monthly release providing comprehensive data on U.S. trade balance, exports, and imports. It covers physical goods and services, measuring international transactions.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services (FT-900): Dataset Report

*Research current as of October 9, 2026. The latest release covers August 2026 and came out October 6, 2026.*

---

## 1. Checking your title and description

Your title and description are basically correct. A few corrections and additions would make them more precise:

| Element | Your version | What I found |
|---|---|---|
| Title | "US International Trade in Goods and Services" | The official title is **"U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services."** The Census Bureau report number is **FT-900** (also written FT900). The release is sometimes informally called the "trade report" or "trade deficit report." |
| Publisher | Not stated | It is a **joint release of two agencies**, both in the Department of Commerce: the **U.S. Census Bureau** (goods) and the **Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)** (services, plus adjustments that convert the goods data into balance-of-payments terms). Each release has two numbers. For example, the August 2026 release is BEA 26-44 / CB 26-160. |
| "Monthly release" | Correct | It comes out monthly at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, about 35 days after the month ends. It is embargoed until release. |
| "Comprehensive data on trade balance, exports, imports" | Mostly correct | The goods data are very detailed: by commodity, country, end-use category, state and port. The services data are much less detailed: 11 broad categories, with country detail only for selected countries and areas. |
| "Physical goods and services" | Mostly correct | "Goods" includes things that aren't ordinary merchandise, such as nonmonetary gold. On a balance-of-payments basis it also includes adjustments, for example software valued at market value and repair services removed. The services statistics are partly survey-based estimates, not complete counts. |
| "Measuring international transactions" | Correct | Precisely, it measures transactions between U.S. residents and residents of other countries. U.S. sales abroad are exports, U.S. purchases are imports, and the difference is the trade balance. |

**Suggested fuller description:** *A monthly joint release of the U.S. Census Bureau and BEA. It reports U.S. exports, imports and the trade balance for goods (from administrative customs and export filings) and services (from BEA surveys and other sources). Figures are seasonally adjusted, in current dollars, with detail by end-use commodity category, selected countries and areas, and services type. Goods are presented on both a "Census basis" and a "balance of payments basis."*

---

## 2. Who publishes it

**U.S. Census Bureau, Economic Indicators Division, International Trade**
- Compiles the goods statistics from import and export filings collected through U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) systems.
- Goods data inquiries: 301-763-2311 or (800) 549-0595 option 4; eid.international.trade.data@census.gov
- Media: Public Information Office, 301-763-3030, pio@census.gov
- Main pages: census.gov/ft900 and census.gov/foreign-trade

## 3. Legal authority and mandate

**Goods (Census Bureau)**
- **13 U.S.C. Chapter 9, §§301–307.** Section 301(a) authorizes the Secretary of Commerce to collect information from everyone exporting from or importing into the U.S. and to "compile and publish such information pertaining to exports, imports, trade, and transportation."
- **13 U.S.C. §301(b)** requires the Secretary to send the House Ways and Means Committee and the Senate Finance Committee quarterly and cumulative import and export statistics by country and product.
- **13 U.S.C. §301(g)** makes Shipper's Export Declarations and their electronic successor, Electronic Export Information (EEI), exempt from public disclosure unless the Secretary decides that would be against the national interest. This is why record-level data are not public.
- **13 U.S.C. §301(h)**, added by Pub. L. 107-228 (2002), authorizes mandatory electronic export filing through AES.
- **Foreign Trade Regulations (FTR), 15 CFR Part 30.** These rules govern EEI filing in AES and are the foundation for the export statistics. EEI is also used for export control.

**Services (BEA)**
- **International Investment and Trade in Services Survey Act**, 22 U.S.C. §3101 et seq. Originally the International Investment Survey Act of 1976, it was broadened in 1984 and renamed. The 1984 change made reporting on services transactions mandatory; before that it had been largely voluntary.

**Statistical-policy framework**
- It is a **Principal Federal Economic Indicator**. That means release timing, embargo and pre-release access follow OMB Statistical Policy Directives No. 3 and No. 4, and release dates are set a year ahead.
- Both Census and BEA are recognized federal statistical agencies. They are covered by the Evidence Act/CIPSEA framework and OMB's 2024 "Trust Regulation" (5 CFR Part 1321) on the basic responsibilities of statistical agencies. I am confident of this general framework, but you should confirm exactly how each provision applies.

## 5. What the release contains

**Current snapshot (August 2026, seasonally adjusted, balance-of-payments basis)**
- Deficit: $105.6 billion, up $12.7 billion from July's revised $92.8 billion.
- Exports: $315.2 billion. Imports: $420.8 billion.
- Goods deficit: $136.6 billion. Services surplus: $31.0 billion.
- Year to date, the deficit is down $138.2 billion (19.9%) from the same period in 2025.

**Full-year 2025:** first reported as $901.5 billion on Feb. 19, 2026. It now stands at about $932.0 billion after the January-data revision and the June 2026 annual revision.

**Contents**
- About 20+ numbered tables ("exhibits"). They cover:
  - totals and three-month moving averages
  - goods by end-use category and by commodity
  - "real" goods in chained 2017 dollars (Census basis only)
  - petroleum versus non-petroleum goods
  - goods by selected countries and areas, both seasonally adjusted and not
  - services by type
  - Advanced Technology Products
- The release includes detailed explanatory notes on sources, definitions, revisions and errors.

**Two bases for goods**
- **Census basis:** taken directly from customs and export filings.
- **Balance-of-payments basis:** BEA adjusts the Census figures to match international accounting rules. For example, it removes equipment repairs and adds software at market value, certain military transfers and electricity trade with Mexico.

**Services**
- Covers 11 categories: maintenance and repair; transport; travel; construction; insurance; financial; charges for use of intellectual property; telecommunications, computer and information services; other business services; personal, cultural and recreational services; and government goods and services not included elsewhere.
- Based on BEA's quarterly, annual and 5-year benchmark surveys plus other monthly indicators.
- Where no monthly data exist, BEA converts quarterly figures to monthly ones with a standard interpolation method (modified Denton).

**Geographic scope:** the 50 states, D.C., Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and other U.S. territories. Transactions with U.S. military, diplomatic and consular installations abroad are excluded.

**Related products**
- *Advance Economic Indicators Report:* an earlier, high-level look at goods trade, about a week before the full release.
- *U.S. International Transactions* (BEA, quarterly).
- *Annual Revision* release, each June.
- Supporting reports such as the Exhibit history files and the state and port data.

## 6. Method and quality notes for data scientists

1. **Goods data are a complete count, not a sample.** They come from all CBP-collected filings, so there is no sampling error. There are still errors of other kinds:
   - reporting mistakes, mostly in commodity codes and quantities
   - shipments that were never filed, especially exports
   - late filings
   - data-entry errors
   - estimated low-value shipments: exports of $2,500 or less and imports of $2,000 or less (or $250 for certain quota items) are estimated from historical ratios
   
   The reference on these errors is Census's *U.S. Merchandise Trade Statistics: A Quality Profile* (October 2014).
2. **Exports to Canada come from Canada's import data.** This happens under a memorandum of understanding among Census, CBP, CBSA and Statistics Canada. It requires adjustments for coverage, valuation, re-exports and exchange rates. For example, inland freight was 1.5% of export value to Canada in August 2026.
3. **Revisions follow a fixed schedule:**
   - **Goods:** the prior month is revised every month, and there is an annual revision each June.
   - **Services:** the prior month is revised every month. The March, June, September and December releases revise the previous six months. The June annual revision can go back decades, as in 2026, back to 1999.
   - **December and January data releases:** the prior year's seasonally adjusted months are re-benchmarked to match annual totals.
   
   **Always save copies of each release (vintages).** Revised data replace earlier figures.
4. **Most figures are in current dollars,** except the Census-basis real goods table. Headline numbers are seasonally adjusted. Seasonal adjustment by country covers selected countries only, and BEA has an FAQ on it.
5. **Gold distorts the data.** Nonmonetary gold swings heavily, as with the 2025 surges tied to Switzerland. When BEA builds GDP, it replaces gold exports and imports with an adjustment based on domestic gold production minus industrial use. So FT-900 net exports will not exactly match GDP net exports.
6. **Bilateral balances can mislead.** Goods-only balances leave out services surpluses. FactCheck.org (Aug. 2025) showed that a roughly $38 billion goods deficit with Switzerland in 2024 shrank to about $8.6 billion once services were included. Comparing U.S. figures with a partner's mirror figures (such as China's) shows gaps caused by valuation, timing and country-of-origin rules.
7. **Country attribution:** imports are credited to the country of origin and exports to the country of destination. Imports are available as both "general" and "for consumption" figures, and at customs value or CIF value (including cost, insurance and freight).
8. **Things to watch:** tariff-driven stockpiling ahead of tariffs (2025), changes to the de minimis treatment of low-value parcels, and legal challenges to tariffs may affect how imports are recorded and how well the low-value estimates hold up. I found no official notice quantifying these effects, so treat this as something to monitor, not a documented problem.

## 7. How to access the data (for librarians and preservationists)

**Release files**

**APIs and tools**

1. Each month's PDF and XLSX, since revisions overwrite earlier numbers.

## 9. Benefits to the public

- **Accountability on trade policy.** It is the authoritative, nonpartisan measure for judging tariffs, trade agreements and claims about trade deficits, including correcting goods-only claims.
- **Better economic measurement.** Net exports feed into GDP, and the advance goods data were created specifically to improve the first GDP estimate and reduce later revisions.
- **Informed decisions.** It helps businesses, workers and communities understand exposure to foreign markets and supply chains.
- **Transparency and equal access.** Release dates are set in advance and data are published simultaneously for everyone, so no one gets early access. Tools and APIs are free.
- **Long history.** Monthly series stretch back to 1866, which supports historical research.
- **Privacy protection.** Aggregates are published while firm-level filings stay confidential.

---

## 10. Issues for policy advocates

- **Exposure to shutdowns.** The 2025 funding lapse delayed several months of releases and pushed back GDP, international transactions and other reports. Earlier funding lapses have also disrupted releases.
- **Political attention.** Trade balances are central to tariff justifications. That makes the statistics' independence, documentation and long-term preservation especially important.
- **Gaps in services data.** Services are about a third of exports but are estimated with less detail and less timeliness, and are revised heavily. The 2026 revision raised the services surplus for 1999–2024 by an average of 12.8%. Funding for BEA's surveys matters for accuracy.
- **Budgets and modernization.** Both agencies depend on their budgets and on CBP's IT systems (ACE/AES).

*Assessed October 9, 2026. Joint release of the Census Bureau (goods) and the Bureau of Economic Analysis, or BEA (services).*

The release itself is in good shape: the archive is intact, the legal basis is strong, and it has been published on schedule since early 2026. The real risks are deeper down: lost staff, shrinking budgets, leadership changes at Census, and policy shifts that change the underlying import data.

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for "No Known Issue"**
- Census's FT-900 archive (census.gov/foreign-trade/Press-Release/ft900_index.html) still holds every monthly release in PDF and Excel back to 1991, plus each annual revision.

**Evidence that might point to higher risk**

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk"**
- The October–November 2025 government shutdown delayed several releases:
  - October 2025 data came out January 8, 2026 instead of December 4.
  - November 2025 data came out January 29, 2026 instead of January 8.
  - December and full-year 2025 came out February 19, 2026.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for "No Known Issue" (detail maintained or improved)**
- **July 2025:** BEA expanded yearly services detail from 90 to 237 countries and areas, added more detail for some service types, and removed a two-year lag in one table.
- **June 2026:** the annual revision improved how transport services are measured.
- **March 2026:** Census replaced its free trade-data tool with a new version ("USA Trade Online: Reimagined").
- Census plans a proposed rule to add **country of origin** to export filings (91 FR 3102).
- Release frequency (monthly) and timing (about 35 days after the month ends) are unchanged.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk" (possible future loss of detail)**
- BEA's FY2026 budget cut 80 positions and $6.55 million from its national, regional and international accounts. BEA said this "may impact... the level of detail for statistics provided by BEA" (FY2026 budget submission).
- Staff losses at both agencies (see section 5) put reviews, quality checks and methods work at risk. In its 2026 Midyear Update, the ASA reported that agencies have "largely maintained their regular release schedules," but also reported discontinued products and slower modernization.
- **Executive Order 14324**, effective August 29, 2025, ended duty-free treatment for low-value imports. Most of these packages must now be formally declared in the customs system (90 FR, Sept. 2, 2025). This changes the records Census uses to estimate low-value imports, which relies on historical patterns. Coverage might improve, but the break in the series hasn't been measured publicly. Postal shipments still have their own process.
- BEA could not buy IRS tax data for its 2025 annual update. That affected GDP, not trade, but it shows how budget limits can weaken source data.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** No actual loss of detail, timeliness or frequency has happened in FT-900, and some parts have improved. But both the budget documents and staffing levels point to emerging risk.
